programs.title: Posture correction
cautions: Pain, numbness or a lasting problem: see a clinician.
notes: Tensor fasciae latae is not in this anatomy model.

evidence.claim: The evidence that exercise changes standing posture is mixed.
Commonly used in practice. No trial is cited for this item.

items.name: Chin tuck
cues: Sit or stand tall.
Slide the chin straight back, as if making a double chin.
Hold briefly, then relax.

items.name: Deep neck flexor hold
cues: Lie on your back, head supported.
Nod the chin gently without lifting the head.
Hold, breathing normally.

items.name: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae stretch
cues: Sit tall, one hand under the seat.
Tilt the head away and turn the nose toward the armpit.
Hold a gentle stretch. No pain.

items.name: Thoracic extension over a roller
cues: Lie with a foam roller across the upper back.
Support the head with your hands.
Arch gently over the roller, then return.

items.name: Wall slide
cues: Stand with back and forearms on a wall.
Slide the arms up, keeping contact.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Band pull-apart
cues: Hold a band at shoulder height, arms straight.
Pull the band apart, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Return slowly.

parts: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

items.name: Face pull
cues: Hold a rope or band at face height.
Pull toward the face, elbows high and wide.
Return slowly.

parts: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

items.name: Prone Y and T raise
cues: Lie face down, arms in a Y, then in a T.
Lift the arms a little, thumbs up.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Doorway chest stretch
cues: Forearm on a door frame, elbow at shoulder height.
Step through until you feel a gentle stretch across the chest.
Hold, breathing normally.

parts: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle
Clavicular head of pectoralis major muscle

items.name: Dead bug
cues: Lie on your back, arms up, hips and knees bent.
Keep the lower back still.
Lower the opposite arm and leg, then switch.

items.name: Bird dog
cues: Start on hands and knees.
Reach one arm and the opposite leg out, keeping the back level.
Return and switch sides.

items.name: Front plank
cues: Forearms and toes on the floor.
Keep a straight line from head to heels.
Hold, breathing normally.

items.name: Side plank
cues: Lie on one side, forearm under the shoulder.
Lift the hips into a straight line.
Hold, then switch sides.

items.name: Hip hinge drill
cues: Stand with a stick along the back of the head, upper back and tailbone.
Push the hips back, keeping all three contacts.
Stand up by driving the hips forward.

items.name: Side-lying hip abduction
cues: Lie on one side, bottom knee bent.
Lift the top leg, toes pointing forward.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Banded lateral walk
cues: Band around the legs, knees slightly bent.
Step sideways, keeping the knees over the toes.
Keep tension on the band.

items.name: Single-leg squat to a box
cues: Stand on one leg in front of a box.
Sit back to touch the box, knee over the toes.
Stand up without letting the knee drift in.

items.name: Short-foot drill
cues: Sit or stand, foot flat.
Draw the ball of the foot toward the heel to raise the arch.
Keep the toes relaxed. Hold, then relax.

items.name: Calf raise with slow lowering
cues: Stand on the edge of a step.
Rise onto the toes.
Lower slowly over a few seconds.

items.name: Towel curl
cues: Sit with a towel under the foot.
Curl the toes to pull the towel in.
Relax and repeat.

programs.title: Anterior pelvic tilt
cautions: Pain, numbness or a lasting problem: see a clinician.

evidence.claim: Pelvic tilt varies between people, a forward tilt is common, and it often comes with no pain.
Commonly used in practice. No trial is cited for this item.

items.name: Half-kneeling hip flexor stretch
items.component: Lengthen the front of the hip
cues: Kneel on one knee, other foot in front.
Tuck the pelvis under and shift forward a little.
Hold a gentle stretch at the front of the hip.

items.name: Couch stretch
items.component: Lengthen the front of the hip
cues: Kneel with the back foot raised against a wall or couch.
Tuck the pelvis and lift the chest.
Hold a gentle stretch at the front of the thigh.

items.name: Glute bridge
items.component: Strengthen what tilts the pelvis back
cues: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat.
Tuck the pelvis, then lift the hips.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Hip thrust
items.component: Strengthen what tilts the pelvis back
cues: Upper back on a bench, feet flat.
Drive the hips up until the body is level.
Lower with control.

items.name: Dead bug
items.component: Strengthen what tilts the pelvis back
cues: Lie on your back, arms up, hips and knees bent.
Keep the lower back on the floor.
Lower the opposite arm and leg, then switch.

items.name: Reverse crunch
items.component: Strengthen what tilts the pelvis back
cues: Lie on your back, knees bent toward the chest.
Curl the pelvis up off the floor.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Plank with pelvis tucked
items.component: Strengthen what tilts the pelvis back
cues: Forearms and toes on the floor.
Tuck the pelvis and squeeze the buttocks.
Hold, breathing normally.

items.name: Romanian deadlift
cues: Stand holding a weight, knees soft.
Push the hips back, keeping the back flat.
Stand up by driving the hips forward.

items.name: Hamstring curl
cues: Lie face down or use a machine.
Bend the knee against resistance.
Lower slowly.

items.name: Pelvic tilt practice (standing and lying)
cues: Lying, then standing.
Tilt the pelvis forward, then back.
Find the middle and rest there.

programs.title: Pelvic floor
cautions: Pain, numbness or a lasting problem: see a clinician.
Do not stop urine mid-flow as an exercise.
Pain or symptoms getting worse: stop and see a pelvic health physiotherapist.
During pregnancy and after birth, check with a clinician before starting.

evidence.claim: For women with stress urinary incontinence, pelvic floor training made a reported cure about eight times more likely than no treatment (Cochrane review, 31 trials).

source.title: Dumoulin, Cacciari and Hay-Smith 2018, Cochrane CD005654

evidence.claim: For people whose pelvic floor is tense, relaxing matters more than squeezing.
Commonly used in practice. No trial is cited for this item.

items.name: Find the muscles
cues: Sit or lie comfortably.
Squeeze as if holding in wind, and lift inward.
Let go fully. Keep breathing; buttocks and thighs stay relaxed.

items.name: Slow holds
cues: Squeeze and lift.
Hold, then relax fully for the same time.
Build the hold up gradually.

dose.frequency: 3 times a day, for at least 3 months (guideline minimum)

items.name: Quick squeezes
cues: Squeeze and lift quickly and strongly.
Let go fully between squeezes.

dose.frequency: 3 times a day, for at least 3 months (guideline minimum)

items.name: Progress: lying, sitting, standing, during a lift or cough
cues: Start lying down.
Then sitting, then standing.
Then squeeze just before and during a lift or a cough.

items.name: Diaphragmatic breathing
cues: Lie or sit comfortably, one hand on the belly.
Breathe in slowly and let the belly and pelvic floor soften.
Breathe out gently.

items.name: Deep squat hold
cues: Lower into a deep squat, heels down if you can.
Hold onto support if needed.
Breathe slowly and let the pelvic floor relax.

items.name: Happy-baby pose
cues: Lie on your back and hold the feet or shins, knees wide.
Let the knees drop toward the armpits.
Breathe slowly and relax.

programs.title: Sexual health (male)
cautions: Pain, numbness or a lasting problem: see a clinician.
Erection problems that last can be an early sign of heart, blood-vessel or blood-sugar disease. See a doctor.
No exercise makes the penis longer or larger.
Do not stop urine mid-flow as an exercise.
notes: Bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus are not in this anatomy model. The pelvic floor region is shown instead.

evidence.claim: A systematic review of 10 trials found pelvic floor training appears effective for erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation. Trial quality was low to moderate and no best protocol is known.
A meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (1,147 men) found erectile function scores improved by 2.8 points on a 6–30 scale, more in men who started lower.

source.title: Khera, Bhattacharyya and Miller 2023, Journal of Sexual Medicine 20(12)

evidence.claim: Whole-body strength work supports general health.
Commonly used in practice. No trial is cited for this item.

items.name: Slow holds
cues: Squeeze and lift.
Hold, then relax fully for the same time.
Build the hold up gradually.

items.name: Quick squeezes
cues: Squeeze and lift quickly and strongly.
Let go fully between squeezes.

items.name: Control practice
cues: Practise squeezing and fully relaxing on purpose.
Notice the difference between the two.
Keep breathing throughout.

items.name: Brisk walking
cues: Walk fast enough to breathe harder but still talk.

dose.frequency: 150–300 min a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 min of vigorous activity, or a mix (weekly total for all aerobic activity)

source.title: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020)

items.name: Cycling
cues: Ride at a steady pace that raises your breathing.

dose.frequency: 150–300 min a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 min of vigorous activity, or a mix (weekly total for all aerobic activity)

source.title: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020)

items.name: Running
cues: Run at a pace you can keep. Build time up gradually.

dose.frequency: 150–300 min a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 min of vigorous activity, or a mix (weekly total for all aerobic activity)

source.title: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020)

items.name: Swimming
cues: Swim steady lengths at a pace that raises your breathing.

dose.frequency: 150–300 min a week of moderate aerobic activity, or 75–150 min of vigorous activity, or a mix (weekly total for all aerobic activity)

source.title: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020)

items.name: Whole-body strength work
cues: Work all major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, chest, shoulders, arms and trunk.
Use a load you can lift with good form.

dose.frequency: 2 or more days a week, all major muscle groups, moderate or greater effort

source.title: WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (Bull et al., Br J Sports Med 2020)

programs.title: Sexual health (female)
cautions: Pain, numbness or a lasting problem: see a clinician.
During pregnancy and after birth, check with a clinician before starting.
Pain: see a pelvic health physiotherapist.
notes: Female anatomy here is adapted from the male model; pelvic organs are simplified.

evidence.claim: The same Cochrane review reports better sexual outcomes in the pelvic floor training groups.

source.title: Dumoulin, Cacciari and Hay-Smith 2018, Cochrane CD005654

Aerobic and strength work support general fitness.
